title: How does sealing improve `instanceof` checks and exhaustive `switch` pattern matching?
shortTitle: How does sealing improve `instanceof` checks and exhaustive `switch` pattern matching?
topicTitle: How does sealing improve `instanceof` checks and exhaustive `switch` pattern mat

s1_definition.profdef: Sealing gives the compiler complete knowledge of the finite set of subtypes of a type. This lets a `switch` over a sealed type be checked for exhaustiveness: if every permitted subtype is covered, the switch needs no `default` branch, and if a subtype is missing, compilation fails. Combined with pattern matching, `instanceof` and `switch` patterns become safer because the compiler can reason about the closed set, enabling exhaustive type-based dispatch without a fallback and catching unhandled cases at compile time rather than at runtime.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed, closed list of exactly three account products. Because the list is closed and head office knows every entry, a clerk processing accounts can write a checklist with one row per product and be certain the checklist is complete — there is no mysterious fourth product that could slip through unhandled. If someone later adds a fourth product to the official list, every checklist in the bank that is now incomplete is immediately flagged for update. Sealing is what makes the list closed and known, so the checklists can be provably complete.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sealing makes the subtype set finite and known, so the compiler can prove a `switch` is exhaustive and force you to handle every case without a `default`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sealing gives the compiler complete knowledge of the finite set of subtypes of a type. This lets a `switch` over a sealed type be checked for exhaustiveness: if every permitted subtype is covered, the switch needs no `default` branch, and if a subtype is missing, compilation fails. Combined with pattern matching, `instanceof` and `switch` patterns become safer because the compiler can reason about the closed set, enabling exhaustive type-based dispatch without a fallback and catching unhandled cases at compile time rather than at runtime.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed, closed list of exactly three account products. Because the list is closed and head office knows every entry, a clerk processing accounts can write a checklist with one row per product and be certain the checklist is complete — there is no mysterious fourth product that could slip through unhandled. If someone later adds a fourth product to the official list, every checklist in the bank that is now incomplete is immediately flagged for update. Sealing is what makes the list closed and known, so the checklists can be provably complete.

**One line to remember:** Sealing makes the subtype set finite and known, so the compiler can prove a `switch` is exhaustive and force you to handle every case without a `default`.

sections.s2_technical:
Before sealed types, a type could be extended by anyone, anywhere, so the compiler could never be sure it knew all subtypes. That meant a `switch` or chain of `instanceof` checks over subtypes always needed a `default` or `else` to handle "some unknown subtype," even if you believed you had covered them all. If a new subtype appeared, the `default` would silently swallow it, often causing a subtle runtime bug.

**Sealing changes this** by giving the compiler the complete, finite list of permitted subtypes. Now when you write a `switch` over a sealed type with a case for each permitted subtype, the compiler can verify that **every** possible subtype is handled, which is called **exhaustiveness checking**. If the switch is exhaustive, you do **not** need a `default` branch. For example, a `switch` on a sealed `Account` with cases for `SavingsAccount`, `CurrentAccount`, and `LoanAccount` is complete, and the compiler accepts it without `default`.

The real power appears when the **sealed set changes**. If a developer adds a new permitted subtype to the sealed type, every exhaustive `switch` that does not handle the new subtype now **fails to compile**. This turns a dangerous runtime gap into a compile-time error, so the compiler itself reminds you to update every place that dispatches on the type. In a bank, where forgetting to handle a new account product or transaction state could cause financial errors, this guarantee is extremely valuable.

For **`instanceof` with pattern matching**, sealing helps the compiler reason about type coverage. Pattern matching for `instanceof` lets you write `if (a instanceof SavingsAccount s) { ... }` and bind `s` directly. When this is used in an if-else chain over a sealed type, while the language still requires a final `else` for an if-chain, the closed set documents and bounds the possibilities, and modern `switch` patterns supersede the chain with true exhaustiveness. Switch patterns also support **guarded patterns** and **null handling**, and over a sealed type the compiler knows the universe of cases, enabling precise, safe dispatch.

A senior nuance is that exhaustiveness interacts with **sealed hierarchies that are multi-level**: if a permitted subtype is itself sealed, the compiler expands the set transitively, so you can either switch on the intermediate sealed type or on its leaves, and exhaustiveness is computed over the full closed tree. Another nuance is that if you do add a `default` to an exhaustive sealed switch, you lose the compile-time safety net, because the `default` would absorb any new subtype silently, so for sealed types you deliberately omit `default` to keep the guarantee. A final nuance is that this pairing of sealed types with pattern-matching switches is Java's realisation of algebraic-data-type pattern matching found in functional languages, giving banking domain models both closed-set safety and concise, exhaustive dispatch, which reduces whole classes of "unhandled case" defects.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India dispatches different logic based on the transaction result type, and in the past used a `default` branch that silently mishandled any new result type, causing a production incident. The bank wants the compiler to force every dispatch site to handle every result. Sealing plus an exhaustive switch provides this.

Problem 2 — The bank needs type-based extraction of data from each result, such as the amount from an approved result or the reason from a declined one, done safely without casts. Pattern matching in the switch binds the concrete type and its record components directly, avoiding manual casting and the risk of `ClassCastException`.

Problem 3 — The bank wants a guarantee that when a new result type is introduced later, the build breaks at every switch that does not handle it, so nothing is missed. We show that removing a case causes a compile error, proving the safety net.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `TransactionResult` with record subtypes `Approved`, `Declined`, and `Pending`, write an exhaustive pattern switch with no `default`, use record patterns to extract fields, add a guarded pattern for a high-value approval, and log the dispatch, with comments showing the compile-time error if a case is removed.

The code contains: the sealed result type, record subtypes, a `ResultDispatcher` with an exhaustive guarded switch, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four results — an approved transfer of 50,000, an approved high-value transfer of 1,500,000, a declined transfer, and a pending transfer.

Step 1 — The compiler sees the sealed `TransactionResult` and its three record subtypes in the same file, inferring the permitted set. It then checks the `dispatch` switch and confirms it covers all three subtypes, so no `default` is needed. The build succeeds precisely because the switch is exhaustive over the closed set.

Step 2 — `main` dispatches each result. For the first approved result of 50,000, the guarded high-value case does not match because the amount is below one million, so it falls to the plain approved case, which uses a record pattern to bind the reference and amount directly without any cast.

Step 3 — The second approved result of 1,500,000 matches the guarded case `when amount >= 1,000,000`, so it is routed to the high-value compliance-review branch. This shows guarded patterns refining dispatch within the closed set.

Step 4 — The declined result matches its record pattern, binding reference and reason. The pending result matches its record pattern, binding reference and note. No cast and no risk of `ClassCastException`, because the pattern match both tests and binds in one step.

Step 5 — Each dispatch string is logged. If a developer later added a new permitted result type and forgot a case, this switch would fail to compile, catching the omission before deployment.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] APPROVED TXF-1 Rs.50000
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] APPROVED-HIGHVALUE TXF-2 Rs.1500000 (compliance review)
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] DECLINED TXF-3 reason=Insufficient funds
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] PENDING  TXF-4 note=Awaiting OTP
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sealing improves instanceof and switch pattern matching by giving the compiler complete knowledge of the finite set of subtypes. Before sealed types, any type could be extended by anyone, so the compiler could never be sure it knew all subtypes, which meant a switch or an instanceof chain over subtypes always needed a default or else to cover some unknown subtype, and that default would silently swallow any new subtype and cause subtle runtime bugs.

With sealing, the compiler has the exact, closed list of permitted subtypes, so it can check exhaustiveness. When my switch has a case for each permitted subtype, the compiler verifies that every possibility is covered, and I do not need a default branch at all. In my banking project my transaction result is a sealed interface with approved, declined, and pending record subtypes, and my dispatcher switches over all three with no default, which compiles precisely because it is provably complete.

The real power shows up when the set changes. If a teammate adds a new permitted subtype, every exhaustive switch that does not handle it now fails to compile, so the compiler itself points me to every dispatch site that needs updating. That turns a dangerous runtime gap into a compile-time error, which in a bank is enormously valuable because forgetting to handle a new transaction state or account product could cause financial errors. For that reason I deliberately omit the default on a sealed switch, because adding one would hide the safety net by absorbing new subtypes silently.

Pattern matching makes it even better. With record patterns I bind the components directly in each case, so I extract the amount from an approved result or the reason from a declined one without any cast and without risk of a class-cast exception, since the match tests and binds in one step. I also use guarded patterns with when to refine within the closed set, for example routing high-value approvals to a compliance branch. So the combination of sealed types and pattern-matching switches gives me closed-set safety and concise, exhaustive dispatch, which eliminates a whole class of unhandled-case defects, and it is Java's version of the algebraic-data-type pattern matching you see in functional languages.
